method: XGBClassifier (xgboost 3.4.1) on slope-decile-matched negatives; validated with GroupKFold over 0.5 deg spatial blocks
auc_note: auc_spatial_cv is the honest figure. auc_random_cv is inflated by spatial autocorrelation between neighbouring cells and is reported only to show the size of that inflation.
landslide_date_range: 1995-05-22 .. 2026-07-13 (1374 of 9788 records carry a day-precision date; 9533 carry a year)
data_sources: OpenTopoData SRTM 30 m - elevation sampled at 0.025 deg; slope, aspect, relief, TPI, roughness and curvature derived from it
OpenStreetMap via Overpass - state and district boundaries, settlements and population tags
NE_India_Terrain_Features.csv - point terrain at inventory locations (cross-check only; it is the inventory itself, not a grid)
caveats: NE_India_Terrain_Features.csv is the landslide inventory with terrain columns appended, not a prediction grid: all 9788 rows are label=1. The prediction surface here was therefore built from a DEM fetched for the study area.
Susceptibility is static terrain-based likelihood. It is not a forecast and carries no timing.

Slope is scale-dependent. Grid slope here is derived on a ~2.8 km baseline (0.025 deg DEM sampling) and so reads lower than the slope_degrees column in NE_India_Terrain_Features.csv, which came from a fine DEM at point locations. The two are not directly comparable; the min_slope_deg threshold and the slope deciles both refer to the grid-scale value.
Inventory coverage is uneven between states, so absolute probabilities are better read as a ranking than as true frequencies.

The modelled surface is clipped to the eight states the GSI inventory covers. The requested bbox also spans Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, China and parts of West Bengal/Bihar/Jharkhand; those cells were excluded because no survey covers them, so their absence of records is not evidence of stability.
